utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Tuesday, September the 16th, 2008. I would like to greet the accused, the Defence teams, Mr. Stringer and his colleagues from the Prosecution, and I would like also to greet everybody else assisting us in this proceedings, Mr. Registrar and Madam Usher. I would like to give a very short oral decision, but before that I would like to give the floor to Mr. Registrar, who is going to give us an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted an amended version of documents tendered via Martin Raguz. This corrigendum shall be given Exhibit number IC00842. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Very well. A short decision, oral decision, as I said, following a decision by the Appeals Chamber on translation problems. The Chamber by an order of 11th September, 2008, has ordered the translation service of the Registry, CLSS, that a review of the translation be transmitted to it by the 15th of September, 2008. Given the fact that this review can only be transmitted to it today, the Chamber permits the Praljak Defence and, if necessary, the other Defence teams to transmit to the Chamber their observations by the 22nd of September and not by the 18th of September, as initially requested, via our decision of 11 September 2008, which means that you have until the 22nd of September to submit your observations. The examination-in-chief will continue. The Prlic Defence has used up two hours and thirty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. And it may be necessary to go beyond the three hours projected, which, of course, will be taken out of our overall time. We'll just have to make some further adjustments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puljic. How are you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's look at 1D 01217. That's the next document. 1D 01217. We're going to move rather quickly through these documents. This is dated June 1992 in Mostar, and this is a report on the realisation of the civilian protection task in the territory of the town of Mostar during 60 days of war. Do you have the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could look at page 2 in the English version. This would be under item number 1. It's sort of the fifth paragraph. I'm just going to read parts of it and ask you whether you can help us out here. It says that: "Since the work of the civilian authorities was not organised at the beginning of the war, the municipal civilian protection staff took over some powers in order to protect personnel and material and technical goods, and for this reason it formed special-purpose units, which rallied certain profiles of professional staff, especially craftsmen. The purpose was to provide adequate services to all town structures, and this proved to be a very functional and rational move." Do you know whether this is accurate?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we go -- at the very last paragraph under item 1, it says: "However, in spite of these achievements, it must be said that its work especially at the beginning of the war, these appeared to be" -- "there appeared to be confusion, lack of coordination, inadequate level of equipment," which is still the case, "poor connectivity and lack of subordination, et cetera. However, all these problems were eliminated as time went by, resulting in more complete functioning of the overall system of civilian protection." Is that accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. If we look at the very last page, is there a signature there, and if so, can you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognize the signature, but I assume that it's the commander or the deputy commander of the Civilian Protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, which is 1D 0579, and along with this document we will go through a series of other documents related to appointments, and this may be useful concerning one of the questions posed to you yesterday. 1D 00579. This is a decision on the establishment and tasks of the Mostar municipal HVO commissioners in setting up managing functions of the socially-owned companies and institutions in the Mostar municipality under wartime conditions. Are you familiar with this decision, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I won't go into -- I won't ask you what is a commissioner since it's laid out in this document, and of course, the members of the Bench can ask you questions on that. But if we look at Article 5, we can see the following spheres. Would you confirm that this actually was implemented, this decision, and commissioners were set up for the various spheres as reflected in Article 5?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And of course, if you go to Article 7, it talks about the management organs of the socially-owned companies and institutions in Mostar municipality shall propose candidates for management positions. And then if we look at number 9, it says: "The company manager shall carry out all activities necessary for the Mostar municipal HVO commissioner to carry out his obligation as determined under Article 2." What exactly did a company manager do, if you could help us out here, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was responsible for the work and the functioning of the company. He would take all steps so that the company would carry out its function. In view of the fact that many directors fled, it was necessary to replace them with other people so that the companies could function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at some appointments, and we'll go very quickly. 1D 00445, this is a decision on appointing of temporary director of the agricultural cooperative Blagaj, and we see the name. Is this individual being appointed, is he a Croat or Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, again, if I may ask you, because I don't want to repeat the question, this is a temporary appointment. Do you know why the appointment is temporary and not permanent?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the expectation was that once the war was over, permanent managerial posts would be set up in the usual, regular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D 00659. 1D 00659, a decision to appoint -- this is to the Blagaj fish farm, that individual being appointed on 3 November 1992, of what nationality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00450. This is 1 December 1992, appointing the temporary director of Unis, E.L. Company Mostar. First of all, what kind of company is this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a socially-owned company, a very important one, and it's a company with a large profit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What does it do, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used to manufacture calculator boards or parts for calculators for the Swedish Erickson company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the individual being appointed, what is he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00452. Again, this is 1 December 1992. This is for the Fashion Clothing Company, a decision appointing a director, a temporary director. And what nationality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 1D 00454, again, December 1. This is temporary director of the D.P. Rad Company. What kind of company is this, by the way; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a construction company that used to perform artisan works mostly on publicly-owned or socially-owned apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this individual?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00456. This is a decision dated 2 December 1992. This is a director of D.P. Clothing Company, and of what nationality is this individual?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00460. This is a decision appointing a temporary director of Sipad Door Factory, 11 December 1992. What nationality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00461. This is 11 December 1992. This is for the temporary appointment, director of Air Industry, RKT Firm. First of all, what kind of industry is this? I know we see the name of it, but what exactly does it do, and how important is it in that area?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first or second company by its importance in Mostar. We had two major companies, Soko and Aluminium. Soko manufactured airplanes and helicopters, and besides that, it manufactured other products such as car parts and parts for cooling equipment and so on and so forth. In any case, they employed 5.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this individual, is he a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00685. 5 January 1993. This is the acting manager of the Toplana Public Enterprise. First of all, what kind of enterprise is this? I mean, what does it do, and how important is it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a public company owned by the municipality, and in view of the fact that practically the entire apartment stock in the buildings had central heating and district heating, joint heating plants, this company was responsible for providing heat to the town in wintertime to make sure that all the apartments were being heated, that the equipment was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And this individual, is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim, since the director left. The original director fled from the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00701. This is dated 19 January 1993. This is appointing an acting director of Herzegovina, Drustveni Standard. I can't pronounce the name. I think I did okay. What does this company do, and who is this individual?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostar had a large construction company called "Herzegovina," and it included or it was made up of a number of smaller companies, and one of those companies provided food for the workers. And in work conditions, when conditions were regular, the company provided food and meals for the city and public cafeteria or a canteen where all those who did not have food were able to come and eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Is this individual a Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Muslim person. He was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00706. This is a decision on appointing temporary director of Herzegovina, Projektni Zavod. What does this company do, and is this person a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that G.P. Herzegovina was a concern comprising a number of companies, and one of those companies was a company that designed that facility or facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00463. This is a decision, 3 February 1993, temporary director, Herzegovina, building construction. You already told us more or less told us about the company. Is this individual a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a Muslim. Unfortunately, he was killed a few days after his appointment in shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And who was responsible for the shelling?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shell came from Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second, Witness. What you've just said is interesting. We are on the 3rd of February, 1993. Mr. Seadin Jahic has been appointed to this position. You've just said he's a Muslim, and you added that five days later he was killed in shelling. The Defence counsel asked you who was responsible for the shelling, and you said the Serbs. In February 1993, there is shelling on Mostar and the Serbs are responsible for such shellings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you know it was the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was nobody else to shell the town. We wouldn't have been shelling ourselves, our own city. Serb positions were at Podvelezje, and they were shelling Mostar from there every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. And to your knowledge, those Serb shellings lasted until when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There wasn't a rule. There would be one, two, three days without shelling. Then there would be shelling. Then a few days after that, there would be no shelling, and that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. And did it last the whole year of 1993? Do you have a date to give us when they stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you an exact date, but the shelling lasted until March or -- February or March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] February or March 1993. And after March 1993, did the Serbs leave the positions they formerly occupied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the Serbs stayed at those positions, but that's when the conflict between Muslims and Croats broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When there was fighting between the Croats and the Muslims, to your knowledge would the Serbs occasionally shell, as well, the area, or did they stop doing anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that they stopped. I'm not entirely sure, but I think that for a while they did stop their shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then the last document that relates to these appointments, at least for now, is 1D 00464, and we can see this is 11 February 1993. Is this individual being appointed as the executive principal of the elementary school in Blagaj, is he a Croat or is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And before I go to any more documents, just another point I want to try to cover. Did the municipal employees, the employees that worked for the municipality, were they fired by the Croats or the HVO in order to rehire an entire new workforce for the municipality? Did that ever occur?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This never happened. The HVO never dismissed workers or employees of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Witness, I mean, you had a specific function in the municipality, but you were not the head of the municipality, nor were you head of personnel or some such position. How can you be so affirmative about what you have just said? Why are you so sure that never a Muslim was - [French spoken] - sent away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm absolutely sure. In my service, there were 72 municipal employees. Most of the other employees, I knew. We would meet in the corridors. We worked on different jobs jointly. I was in Mostar throughout that whole period, and I was with those people. I didn't see or hear and no one ever complained of those people, that they were dismissed from their job, not even a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were 72 municipal employees in your department. Out of the 72, how many were Croats, and how many were Muslims, and how many were Serbs, as the case may be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was approximately the same number of Serbs and Croats -- of Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the same number of Croats and Muslims and a little bit fewer Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are as many Croats as Serbs, there must have been between 20 and 30 Muslims. During that period of time, those 20 to 30 Muslims were never fired? They were always there? Please, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I misspoke or you misunderstood. More or less, there was approximately the same number of Muslims and Croats and fewer Serbs. That's how it was. I might have misspoken, or perhaps I was misunderstood. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I understood you well. You said there were 72 employees. I assume that if there is half-half, they'll be 30 to 35 Croats, 30 to 35 Muslims, and then what's left are between 20 and 30 Muslims [as interpreted]. I was asking you how many Muslims there were, but you can't give me an accurate figure, it seems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can say that there were either 25 or 30 Croats or 25 or 30 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Very well, between 25 and 30 Muslims. So there were 25 or 30 Muslims. They were there for the whole duration of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole service left the building in 1992, early 1992, and moved to a business space on the west bank of the town. I went to the Crisis Staff and was replaced at my original post by Mr. Rozic. Every day, the service was getting smaller and smaller. People were leaving on a daily basis, and so I think in the end, there was maybe a maximum of 15 to 20 persons who actually remained to work in the service. Many women worked there, and they had to leave the town with their children because of the shelling. All the employees who stayed in the service would meet approximately at 9.00 in the morning. They would spend an hour or two at work, and then they would all go their own way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood correctly, the service moved to West Mostar. The staff number decreased because given the events which were taking place, some people preferred to leave. However, it would be interesting to know whether in West Mostar during 1993 there were still a few employees who were also Muslims, Muslims who were still working under the authority of your successor, Mr. Rozic. That's what I would like to know, or if there were only Croats, if all the Muslims had gone.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all Muslims left. Both Muslims and Croats still worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to come back to my question. Mr. Puljic, Mr. Karnavas, and this is the first lines of page 11, asked you whether the employees that worked for the municipality were fired by Croats, and the understanding is Muslim employees for the municipality. You were quite categorical and said that never happened. I asked you, "How do you know?" Your answer was, "I was together with 72 of my service." Now, I absolutely understand that you knew very well what happened there, but what about the rest of the administration? Your service was not the whole administration of the town or even the district of Mostar, I understand. How do you know that in other services it was exactly the same as in your own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had worked for the municipality before the war and knew a great many people who were municipality employees. I'd meet them out in the street, including Muslims. Nobody had ever complained to me of having been sent away from work or about having come into difficulties simply for the fact that he or she was a Muslim. Had such an incident occurred, somebody would have known about it, and I would have heard about it because I was moving in those circles, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. 1D 00590. We see this is dated 3 July 1992. We're on to another subject now, a decision to setting up a public kitchen for indigents in Mostar municipality. We did hear testimony in here where one particular gentleman for the Prosecution had indicated that this reminded -- that even the thought of setting up a public kitchen was sort of a demeaning event, and it reminded him of certain events that occurred in World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What was the purpose of setting up this public kitchen, and how long did it last, and was it restricted to one particular nationality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime, too, there are people who are indigent. Of course, in times of war the numbers of such people increase greatly. At the time in Mostar, there were many people, refugees, who had come to town carrying only a parcel. They either came from Eastern Herzegovina or from the left bank. All of them had to be fed. For this reason, the government launched the action of setting up public kitchens where everybody would have equal access to. Some of those kitchens are still open today. Everyone got a meal in those kitchens. I know that it must have been hard for some people who were quite affluent and then at one point lost all their property and all their belongings and work. It must have been quite difficult to stoop down and to go into one of those kitchens, but it was definitely independent of any ethnic principles. I used to come across a former municipal employee who was a well-reputed land surveyor who used to go to one of those public kitchens every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00594. We see this is a decision -- it's a 24 July 1992 decision to create the post of deputy head in each office of the Croatian Defence Council of the Mostar municipality. Do you know what was the purpose for this particular decision?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you tell us? And we need to move faster, so please tell us.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what this is about. Since we lived in a multiethnic community, in order to ensure ethnic equality, the HVO decided that in addition to heads of offices, all the offices would also have deputies, which made it possible for, let's say, the head of the office to be a Muslim and then his deputy a Croat, or vice versa. All the ethnicities were thus represented as a result of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00601. 25 July 1992. This is a decision on setting up the Mostar municipality Office for Cooperation with Benelux. When I saw this decision, I was wondering, you know, what on earth is this office all about? Could you please help us out here?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people left -- left the area during the war and got a job abroad, found themselves in a position to be able to send humanitarian aid to Mostar. This office was set up in order to deal with the incoming humanitarian aid and in order to provide a legal framework for this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And to your knowledge, were offices set up elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00604. This is a conclusion dated 25 July 1992 on the preparation of a report on illegally-constructed buildings in Mostar. Why was this necessary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many persons started building structures without a legally-issued permit because the municipal offices weren't working properly. That's why the HVO asked that a plan be drawn up of the buildings that can be issued with a permit and those which could not. So this was something that fell into the field of construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 00608. This is a conclusion on the opening of necessary shops that would provide supplies to the population. This is dated 25 July 1992. Why was this necessary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the HVO battalions were territorially deployed and belonged to certain parts of town, members of these battalions knew best which sort of shops were required or needed. So in order to, let's say, prevent furniture shops from being opened where they're not needed and instead ensuring that food shops be opened, this recommendation was made in order to make sure that the situation on the ground was under control.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 01804, and this is dated 5 August 1992. And this is regarding the establishment of electoral "priveda" public enterprise of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. If we look at the end of this document, we see Vladimir Soljic, who is the head of the Department of Economy. Did you know this gentleman? Do you know the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at -- after the first paragraph, it says here: "All organised economic activities and payment transactions in the area of BH have ceased." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "The war is still continuing without an end in sight." Is that correct at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "The BH government is unable to communicate with, let alone act, on a large part of BH territory." Was that correct? I'm looking at the document. This is --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I understand you want to economise time, but it seems to me that this is leading question upon leading question all the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I beg to differ with you, and see, this is part of the problem, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I tell you what my opinion is, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I understand, so -- well, first I haven't heard it in objection, but you're raising it. Fine. But here's the problem that -- for the record for the umpteenth time. During the Prosecution's case, I was not allowed to cross-examination properly. During my case, I don't have sufficient time to put on my evidence. How on earth is Dr. Prlic going to get a fair trial? So I have to resort to these sorts of mechanisms. Now, I'm asking him if this was -- if this accurately reflects the situation. Why do I have to do that? Because you have adopted, along with everyone else, mechanisms for the introduction of documents. In other trials, which I pointed out yesterday in the pleading, in other trials where there seems to be more procedural equality among the accused, they can merely introduce documents very easily. In this particular Chamber, however, the problem is that we get twice -- fewer documents in because of the restrictive measures that you impose. It seems that during the Prosecution's case, I was not allowed to put in evidence, and I filed motion after motion for reconsideration. I was told, "No, put on your case," even though I thought at the time and I still think that it was a violation of my client's rights because he does not have to put on a case, but we're putting on a case. Now that I'm putting on a case, I asked for 150 hours. I was given 97 or whatever. It is virtually impossible for me to defend, and so the perception - and I'm talking about perception - is that when the Defence is not properly allowed to put on its case, the end result can only be a conviction. Now, Mr. Mundis in the Delic case early on, when it began, he moved to have that case transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina under 11 bis because he was not given sufficient time to put on his Prosecution case, claiming - and rightfully so - that if not given sufficient time to put on his case, it would guarantee an acquittal as opposed to letting the facts speak for themselves. So that's the problem that I'm having. Now, I have no other way. I've been doing this for a long period of time. I don't know what the experience is of the Trial Bench of actually trying cases, but I would welcome some pointers on how to better manage my time and put on all this -- these documents in because without the documents, you cannot assess the events. That's the whole problem. The Prosecution is alleging that there's this whole Croatisation of Mostar, that everybody was fired, that positions were changed, that at the top level all the Muslims were removed in order to Croatise these positions. I'm now presenting evidence, hard evidence, from published documents, such as the Official Gazettes, which demonstrate quite to the contrary, albeit it's up to a certain point in time, before the Muslim-Croat conflict in the area, keeping in mind, however, that we have a joint criminal enterprise, what they're alleging that as early as 1991 the process of Croatisation began. So we can't have it both ways, Judge Trechsel. Now, I would welcome some pointers, seriously. How can I do my job better if I have all these documents? What's the sense of me reading all of these documents, selecting the best, going over them with the witness, in order to make your job as efficient as possible, but I cannot do it any other way. Now, you say it's leading. How is it leading? I fail to see how it's leading when I'm asking the gentleman to confirm whether the document reflects the truth because I need that in order for you to accept it. And I must say, with all due regret, that when the Prosecution was putting on its case, it seemed the standard for introduction and admission of evidence to have been slightly lower, and I have to jump much higher. And I can see this because continually my documents are being rejected, even when witnesses are testifying, keeping in mind that we have a procedure here that is based on the continental process where basically it all comes in for you to figure out at the end. We've never had to worry about that, but now when I'm putting on my case, we are, and it's a clarion call to the other accused because they're going to face similar situations as I'm facing. So I'm really at a loss, so help me out here, Judge Trechsel. What can I do to get my documents in within my time period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just make one brief comment. I'm not going to get into the details. We reject much of what Mr. Karnavas has said, particularly the assertion that there's any disparity in the levels or the standards being applied by the Trial Chamber in respect of the procedure or the standards for disability. We reject that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I agree with what you just said. I agree with it. It is true that the Trial Chamber did reject a few documents that you had tendered through some witnesses; and in its decision, the Trial Chamber decided that they would not be admitted as such, but you could re-show them, re-present them to other witnesses because the Trial Chamber estimated that the witness in question had not been able to provide enough information that would allow for the document to be admitted. However, for this witness here, this person who worked at the municipality, as far as Croatisation is concerned, he did say that the municipal employees had not been fired because they were Muslims. You presented a whole series of documents on the appointments, and he did confirm all that. So as far as I'm concerned, there will be no problem regarding this kind of document. But you do have a wealth of documents, so I think that this is the procedure you should follow. You should -- during the proofing session, you should tell the witness, "Okay, we saw 25 documents sitting with one topic. You told me you knew these documents. You knew what their content is," and so forth and so on. "I will show them three or four documents illustrating the whole series." You present them to the witness, ask questions. You see that the Judges systematically also ask questions, sometimes even ask questions that have to do with other topics that you have not dealt with. That's the way it went. And then the 23 documents that you did not present who are in the series and who are identical to the two or three documents that you actually showed the witness should be admitted, as far as I'm concerned. If, unfortunately, these documents end up being rejected, you still have a possibility. You could file a written motion in view of admitting these documents based on our guidelines. But at the end of the case, when the Prosecution will write its final brief and you will write your final brief, in this final brief you can say that as far as Croatisation is concerned, you are challenging this point for the different reasons. You will present your arguments, and as a footnote you will refer to all the documents which actually seem to back what you're saying. And then the Trial Judges will have the two cases in front of them, and then they will verify everything and check everything by looking at the documents that were admitted. Of course, when you ask for important documents to be admitted, please tell us, you know, which ones are totally relevant. It would be impossible to think that documents would not be admitted in this trial even though they have a probative value and back your case because this would be a denial of justice, and of course, I would never allow for this to happen. We're all -- you know, we have no time, of course. None of us have time. You could show us thousands of documents, hundreds of appointments. You could be doing that, but you don't have time for it, unfortunately. So limit yourself, please. Take advantage of the fact that you have this witness that was in such a post, to ask him, "We've seen a good number of documents," and then ask your questions, and there will be a fair trial in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say a few words too. It is, of course -- you're right, Mr. Karnavas, to raise some issues where you disagree with us, with the Chamber, and of course there are issues which are sometimes not very favourable to the Defence or on the other day to the Prosecution, et cetera. There are issues which are, of course, totally debated. On the other hand, I have to say that all major decisions on procedural matters in this Trial Chamber have been also examined and, in a way, adopted by and confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. So therefore, I would like to disagree with you when you said that there is no equality of arms. I definitely have to state that in this Trial Chamber, all the parties are given equal time, equal facilities to work with. And it is what I want to say, and although we may disagree on certain points, we cannot allege -- you cannot allege that here there is a kind of detrimental approach towards the Defence by the Trial Chamber. It is really -- it would lead nowhere to accuse ourselves with this or that kind of behaviour. I would like to call you and call all the parties to go along with the adopted rules and not to raise issues which are not appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A quick response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I wish to respond, especially to Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes. I regret, Mr. Karnavas, that whenever I think that I have to recall some basic rules, you react very defensively and speak as if I wanted to hinder the Defence. I do not. I understand the difficulties you have with these documents, and I'm even prepared to say that we accept the way you put the questions. I just would like it to be clear that it is exceptional, and I would grant the exception, Mr. Karnavas. I absolutely see that it is legitimate for you to present us with these documents, and I also agree that we have created a bit of a difficult system by following the Anglo-Saxon rule that documents should be introduced via witnesses. This is something that is strange to Continental proceedings. I tried to find a compromise there, but please believe me, I do not in any way want to hinder the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, because Judge Prandler talks about procedural fairness. We did not appeal the one issue - and maybe in retrospect, I should have - where repeatedly we said we needed to get our documents in through the Prosecution's case. It's done universally because many times a Defence may choose not to put on a case. Their case is put on through the Prosecution case. And if the Prosecution hasn't put on a case to meet, there's nothing to do. Haradinaj is a very good example where the Defence chose not to put on a case, and Mr. Haradinaj was acquitted. So there is an example. But let me point to one particular example which I find very troublesome, which is why I tried to constantly find ways to get my documents in. There is a series of documents where Mr. Prlic was appointed as the prime minister, after the Medjugorje agreement, where he's making nominations, there are exchanges, and we've heard from numerous witnesses. We've heard from witnesses for the Prosecution side. We also brought in Mr. Akmadzic. We heard it from Mr. Buntic, and repeatedly these same documents, even though they're talking about the events, these witnesses are well aware, repeatedly the Bench rejects them. Frankly, in another setting, in another courtroom in this building, they would accept those. And that's why I talk about procedural inequality, and I find it fundamentally unfair if, in another courtroom, somebody else is getting more procedural rights than my client. Now, it happens to be the nature of the beast of this particular institution that we don't have quite a uniform process because we have Judges coming from all over, different traditions, and each case poses its own individual challenges, and I understand that. But I am concerned, and I take to heart the President's remarks. But what if, after I can't get my documents in through the witness and then I put it through a motion and I still get rejected, how do I make my record? Upon what can I then cite in my final brief if it's not in? If I know anything, and if I learned anything over the last quarter of a century practicing criminal defence work, is I need my record for a variety of reasons, especially for the appeal process because it's well known that lawyers do lose cases. So that's why we tried to do it this way. Now, I'm trying to get -- we have selected what we believe are the best of the best. Frankly, I'm only sharing about 10 per cent of what we go through, and it seems like a lot. But this is, after all, a document case, and Mr. Scott told us that from the very, very beginning, that this is a heavily document-oriented case. It's not so much as to whether this incident happened or that incident, but a lot of this stuff has to do with documents. So if I could just proceed, and I'll try to be a little bit more officious and less leading, if that is the case, and I would welcome further interventions if it appears that my questioning would devalue the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We were speaking about 1D 01804.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just ask you, at that point -- if you could just look at the very last paragraph of this document. It says: "Lastly, it should be pointed out that the observations about the real situation in BH, the identical task of linking power grid segments in the region of HZ-BH and the fact that the power grid in HZ will be connected to the entire power grid of RBH, do not prejudice any political solution after the war and that all that is being done is for the benefit of all citizens of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And I guess my question is: Can you please help us out here? What is he talking about when he says "linking up in the power grid"? How -- do you have sufficient knowledge to help us out on this particular topic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I'm an architect by profession, but my specialty is space planning, and I spent a large part of my life planning physical areas, including the energy grid. When the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the energy supply network simply fell apart because many transmission lines were destroyed. They were physically destroyed, the transmission lines that linked the Bosnia areas with Herzegovina because of the war. A single company, enterprise could no longer function as such as a single entity, and that's why it was necessary to find provisional temporary solutions so that people could continue to have an energy supply and to keep up the regular production levels. And this is exactly what Mr. Soljic was trying to do. As for all of this that he mentions, I was familiar through the engineers in my company who were involved in planning the energy network system and supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very quickly, if we could go through some of these other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second. I have a question to show that the Judges take an interest in your documents. Witness, you said you were a specialist in space planning and that you had some knowledge regarding energy. We have here a document on the issue of power supply. We understood that before the events, there was one single company which was in charge of the power supply at the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that after the events there were power cuts and that you had to find solutions at your own level. I listened to what you said, and I'm wondering if, in 1991, 1992, and 1993, as far as power supply was concerned, you also needed electricity coming from other countries - Germany, Croatia, for example - or if the energy supply system was dependent and working on its own resources.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first task that had to be completed in that sense was to organise the system in such a way, the transmission line system, to fully utilise our own resources, and that means the transmission of energy which was unified in the whole country had to be organised in a different way so as to use our own resources. For example, one hydroelectric power plant that was on our territory perhaps provided energy to a broader area. Now, this was not possible, so all of that energy had to be redirected to us in the same way other power plants that produced energy produced it for who knows which area. So it was a single unified system, and then we had to redirect that, also, that we would direct some for our own area. When there were power cuts, this had to be taken care of. I assume that we exported energy and imported energy, so then this power grid had to be organised in a proper, logical way in the new circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document we have before us, if there hadn't been any agreement with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on power supply, wouldn't that have been a major problem for the territories under Mr. Izetbegovic's control? Those territories were also dependent upon you and the decisions you were making, or as far as the power supply for Sarajevo and other areas, were there other sources of energy? In other words, weren't you all interdependent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in terms of the energy network. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was my question. I think it's a major issue. You were all interdependent. Very well. Let's move on. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just -- I'm going to skip through some documents to save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you look at -- the next document will be 1D 00629, so look for 629. It's right in front of you. This is a decision. It's on 16th September, formally agreeing to the analysis of the consequences, measures and actions to overcome the situation imposed by the war, and essentially if we look at number 2, it says: "The Office of Civilian Protection is hereby tasked with forwarding the approved analysis under item number 1 to all Mostar municipal HVO commissioners ..." Can you please tell us, what was this about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Civilian Protection here made an analysis and proposed measures in this analysis to surmount the situation imposed by conditions of war, and simply the HVO is transferring these assignments to a lower level throughout the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00634. This is a decision on providing funds for heating on the hospital to the city. I'm most interested because this is 16 September 1992. It says, "The funds of 596.400 German marks are hereby allocated." Now, there's been an issue here that one of the methods of Croatising the area was introducing the Croatian dinar. Here we have German marks. Can you please explain to us the situation in Mostar at the time, as you understood it, having lived through the period? Why was German marks being used? Why not use the good old Bosnian dinar, assuming it existed at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav dinar was not being used at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the Bosnian dinar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnian dinar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wasn't there a currency coming out of Mostar, the central bank? Why use German marks? From Sarajevo, wasn't there coming --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This money was not available in the Mostar area. It couldn't -- we couldn't get to it. That money was not used. Physically, it could not reach Mostar from Sarajevo. It wasn't being used. It wasn't available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00442. This is the last document dealing with this segment, and this is a decision on giving the approval of the decision on appointing of management in the Department of Communal Housing Affairs and Reconstruction. And if you could please tell us, are there any Muslims being appointed to this, based on this decision, and who they are?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Nedzad Zvonic, that's number 1; number 3, Ekrem Curic; number 4, Mirza Trbonja; and number -- no, Zora, so three are being appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please just explain very briefly the significance of these appointments, just in a sentence.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are assistants of the chief of this department, and they would carry out the most important work, complete everything. They communicate with the clients, and then together with the desk officers, they would accept the problem, resolve it, and then just go to their boss for the signature. So they are the ones who bear the brunt of the work in the Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another section, and we're going to be dealing primarily with the issue of accommodations. And I want to look first at 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move to accommodations: Witness, in many decisions I've noticed that the municipality was concerned with rebuilding destroyed houses, destroyed during the conflict or conflicts. To your knowledge, the implementation of all those decisions, did it take place during the conflict - in particular, during 1993 - or did the rebuilding in the municipality of Mostar, for example, did it start after the Washington Agreements? Were there any measures which started during the conflict, rebuilding measures, that is, during the year 1993, and do you have one or several examples in which Muslims who had their shops or houses destroyed would have come to the municipality for help, financial help, for instance, so that they could repair their houses or their flats? Do you have such examples to give? Are there any, to your knowledge? Maybe you don't have them, but if you do, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know any examples. I don't know any specific examples, but I do know one thing, and that is that people were repairing their homes as the shells were falling because they had to live somewhere, but the actual true reconstruction began later, after the Washington Agreement, and the municipality tried to monitor the warehouses of construction material and the humanitarian aid that came that consisted of construction material and tried to help that this material is distributed to where it was most needed, to set up a priority, to use the least amount of material to achieve the most effect. I don't know that there was any differentiation along ethnic lines in the delivery of this construction material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the issue of accommodations now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at 1D 02647, this is -- seems to be a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recognise it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, if we look into the second page in English, we see that you're mentioned there as director. Could you please tell us what this study is all about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the director of the public company for the reconstruction and construction of Mostar, I issued an order to a group of engineers to assess the current situation of the destruction in town of habitable facilities and public facilities and to propose measures and means to restore these buildings in order to be able to accommodate refugees and displaced persons there, and that's what they did. This study and this material we used in order to be able to know what to do within the municipality, so it was for us but also as a kind of map to see where we could get help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just very briefly, the Judges may have some questions on this, but if we look at under -- it would be on page 6 in the English version. It's 2.1, the second -- if you look at under number 2, review of the situation after the destruction of Mostar municipality. So that would be Chapter 2; I guess you could call it that, and we see some figures here. And for instance, you see where it talks about public buildings, 80 per cent. These figures, what do these figures represent, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The engineers for the -- from the public company for the reconstruction and construction of Mostar went into the field. They inspected the buildings and made an initial quick assessment of the damage and categorised the buildings. Then they processed the information, and they put it in this table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at 2.2.1, the degree of damage on the housing stock, and we have a table there, and do you see it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to slow down a little bit and articulate your thoughts as best as possible. Could you please explain to us, what exactly does this table represent? And give us -- break it down for us so we can understand it better.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We divided the damage into six categories according to the degree. Then we have the whole housing stock of the town of Mostar, and then we established that in categories 1 to 3, 9.300 apartments in buildings, collective facilities, were destroyed; and in categories 4 to 6 means that they were uninhabitable. There were 700 such apartments. Then houses in the category 1 to 3, 8.300 houses were damaged, while 6.200 houses were unfit for use. And you can say that overall 17.600 housing units in total in the city of Mostar were damaged and 6.900 were destroyed and were absolutely uninhabitable. A large number of the damaged apartments or houses were also unfit for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, are we speaking on the west side, the left side, or the entire city?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the entire city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then, because we don't have enough time to go through this entire report, if we could just focus on page 14, at the very top. It actually begins on page 13. It says: "Minimum necessary intervention and means. Basic costs." It's under 3. -- 3.1. Do you see, you list number 1: "Construction of temporary bridge, construction of temporary pedestrian bridge, and restoration of source Studenac." Could you please explain, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All our efforts were directed towards rebuilding housing so that people would have somewhere to live. In order for them to be able to live but, also, to be able for themselves to help to rebuild, it was necessary to provide electricity, water to these people too. So our assessment here was how much money we needed to build temporary bridges so that the buildings on the left bank would have water and electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And one question I failed to ask you before, but it's a question that has come up with another witness. If you could explain to us - if you know, that is - the percentage of private apartments, privately-owned apartments in Mostar. You know, what is that percentage as opposed to socially owned? And we're talking about at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apartments could be in houses, or they could be in collective buildings. The apartments in houses are 100 per cent privately owned. As for the collective facilities, at that point in time you could have had 1 to 2 per cent of apartments that were privately owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. The next document, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may ask you a question. You have just said it was important to build bridges, so -- or at least one bridge so that water and electricity could be brought to the east bank. Are you saying that the only access of electricity and water to the east bank was across the Neretva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the only way to get to the east side, to cross the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll be covering that, Your Honour, in another segment. 1D 00641. This is just, by way of an example, a decision to grant temporary use of flat, and we see that this is being given to a Maja Cupina -- Majda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does this -- was this sort of a decision a requisite in order for someone to be granted temporary use of a flat? Because yesterday we spoke about the rationalisation of the limited space available.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was essential, and this was the only legal way to get an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00755. This is a decision to provide shelter for refugees, so skip one document, and just go to 1D 00755. If you could just skip a document, Mr. Puljic, please. My time is valuable. I'm asking you to go to 755. Okay. Now, this is, in view of the prevailing situation, the Mostar Hotel - it says "Motel" in English, but it should be "Hotel" - is being used. Where was Hotel Mostar located, on which side?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was being housed there as refugees? Was it -- did you have to belong to one particular ethnicity in order to be housed there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were a refugee, you were given accommodation regardless of your ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 01826. Here we see a report on a working body, and what I'm mostly interested in is under item 3. It talks about University Hall of Residence and Hotel Sokol, that these facilities are available for collective accommodation of expelled persons, refugees and displaced persons, and then, of course, we see the capacity. Did you know these two facilities, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because the Hotel Sokol and the orphans' hall were reconstructed by a public company. They were responsible for rebuilding of these facilities, also the university hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You need to repeat your answer. I'm told that everything was not caught by the interpreters because you were probably speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about these two facilities because the reconstruction projects of the university hall and the Hotel Sokol as well as the overseeing of their reconstruction was conducted by the public company for construction and reconstruction in Mostar, and I know that refugees were accommodated in both of these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you were personally involved? That's the public company that you were managing at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I and my engineers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And finally, P02897. We've seen this document before, and we know that it's been prepared by Mr. Cupina. It's dated 21 June 1993, and what I want you to do is look at, on the first page, under (a), he's proposing certain places for temporary accommodation. Now, before commenting on these places that are listed on the very first page under (a), could you please tell us, what is the situation like in Mostar at this time, June 21, 1993? Is there a conflict, and if so, between whom?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the line of the boulevard, a front was -- a frontline was established, and the two warring sides were in conflict, and it was not possible to cross from one side to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who are the two warring sides?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at the list that's being proposed by Mr. Cupina to the Command of the 4th Corps, the Command of the 31st Glorious Motorised Brigade. And we know from testimony that that's the Muslim armed forces. If we look at this list, and I'm going to go very quickly, the first one, "Aluminium apartment," whose -- under which -- whose side is controlling this, the HVO or the --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Buna Hotel?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Buna Motel?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Buna workers' centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Bacevici?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Hidrogradnja workers' residential area?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Pupils' centre, Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Index students' centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Soko Hotel?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Cernica children's centre?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not going through the next list, which is on page 2 in the English, but having looked at this document, can you please -- and knowing the situation, can you please comment very briefly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that some of the facilities mentioned herein do not exist. For instance, at the time the Energoinvest Hotel didn't exist, practically, because it burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. How realistic is this proposal that he's making to the 4th Corps, that they set up temporary accommodation on territory that is across the boulevard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, absolutely unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the Court, number 3, we note that he's also proposing soup kitchens, and I mention that because of the testimony of that one particular witness I spoke of. Now we're going to go to -- it might be time for the break, Mr. President, and I'll try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, time for the break. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to go to the next topic, which deals with bridges. And I won't go into any great detail with respect to the water and the bridges, but we will discuss that in the next segment of the testimony. 1D 00571, and this is dated 26 June 1992. This is to build -- a decision to build bridges. And if I could focus your attention on Article number 2. It says: "All solutions shall be temporary, pending the creation of conditions for a long-term and effective solution to the problem."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please explain, why was it necessary to have temporary solutions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because under war circumstances and with the shortage of money and resources, you have to find a way of solving a problem in as short a time possible and with as little resources as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we're going to -- at some point, we are going to see some documentation concerning much of the reconstruction that was done, including the bridges, but could you please tell us how many bridges are just in the Mostar city area?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Mostar had 13 bridges at the time. The town proper, on the other hand, had seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of the seven, do you know offhand how many of them were damaged as a result of the initial conflict with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the bridges were damaged -- destroyed, rather. One was damaged, and that was the pedestrian bridge, the old bridge. And another bridge that was outside the town itself remained intact but could not be used because the approach roads to that bridge were destroyed. The terrain -- there was a landslide into the river, and the same workers who had been engaged in the maintenance and the repairing of the bridges were the ones to be selected for this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats broke out, when you had the boulevard as the confrontation line, could you please tell us how many of the bridges in the Mostar city were actually repaired?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, not a single bridge had been repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were efforts being made to repair them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Tito's Bridge at Musala was almost fully repaired, and only the stretch of road of a metre or two needed to be finished. And the Carinski Bridge or the Empire Bridge was ready to be completely prepared, but then as the conflict broke out, none of the two projects could be finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And are these all cement bridges, or are there metal bridges, as well, that you can put together?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The permanent cement bridges were destroyed, and the two were provisional bridges made of steel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's to say the two bridges that we attempted to repair.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you -- well, we'll cover that at some other point. At I understand, Zenica, some parts were -- or portions of the bridge were ordered from Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the Customs Bridge were ordered from Zenica, and they were supposed to be made based on our designs. In addition to that, in Masala, next to Tito's Bridge, we designed a traditional steel bridge, which was to serve as a pedestrian bridge only, and it was also to serve as the passageway for the electrical and gas fittings that were to be placed beneath it. We had made the designs and completed the contract -- or concluded the contract with the Zenica manufacturing company, and had the Zenica manufacturing company done their part of the deal, the bridge would have been repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the transcript says -- on line 16, it refers to gas fittings. Are we talking about electrical and gas fittings or electrical and water fittings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Electricity and water. No, Mostar didn't have gas pipelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, very quickly, 1D 00676. This is a decision for payment of funds of the Mostara Mostar. Just quickly, if you could tell us what is this about. This is December 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A humanitarian concert was organised in Split, which served to raise funds for the reconstruction of the bridges of Mostar. The funds were paid to the HVO in Mostar, who in turn transferred the funds to the public enterprise for that specific purpose of the reconstruction of bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D 02119. This is the last document related to this document, dated April 4, 1993, and it says -- this is a letter that appears to be a "thank you" letter. There is an explanation. It talks about Beily or Beily bridges - I don't know how to pronounce this, Beily bridges - on the Neretva River, and it gives the locations. First, if you could tell us what sort of bridges these are - that's number 1 - and, number 2, where are these locations, and who stands to benefit by installing these bridges?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is being referred to here are Beily bridges. These are military bridges of the type used by all the armies worldwide. They consist simply of a steel structure, which is prefabricated and then fitted together like Lego, and of course, the whole structure serves to span rivers. They are called Beily according to the English engineer who was the first to design that type of bridges. They can be found in the area of Mostar. Avijaticarski Most Bridge was at the very entrance to the town; and then there's Musala in the center of town, that's formerly the Tito's Bridge; and then the Potoci Bridge in the northern part.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes there was another bridge, I didn't catch the name, in the south.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this way, we covered the entire territory or area of the town in order to bring together the two banks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, again, you need to speak slowly. How many bridges are we talking about? Are there three or four? And if you just tell us the locations slowly so we can get it on the record.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were four bridges: Zitomislici, Aerodrom, we call it the Aviator's Bridge, in fact; Musala, formerly Tito's Bridge; and the bridge at Potoci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, are you familiar with this document, and if so, how? Because we don't know to whom this letter is going to. If you look at it, it says "thank you," but we don't have an address. Do you know -- do you have any prior knowledge about this particular document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These bridges were donated to us by the representatives of the American Embassy. A representative of the American Embassy arrived in Mostar and offered from the NATO warehouses in Germany to have bridges transported to the Ploce port in order to connect the two banks of the river. I requested Mr. Prlic to write this letter on our behalf to express our thankfulness to the American Embassy. I took the letter from Mr. Prlic and handed it to the representative of the American Embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if you could tell us when did -- when was it that the American Embassy first made the offer for these bridges?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The representative of the American Embassy came to Mostar in August or September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could go into private session just very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could we please move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could switch now to a topic dealing with water. I'm just going to show you two documents. The Judges may have some questions on this, but the one -- the first one is 1D 01569, and this is addressed to, I see, Jadranko Prlic, July 26, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And any other document that is related, the same subject matter, more or less, is August 4, 1993, and the number of that document is 1D 01566. Now, having looked at these documents, first let me ask you: Are you familiar with how water is supplied to the city of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company I managed was not the company supplying the town of Mostar with water. However, the company did make urban plans, including water supply and the water supply grid, so that I do have an idea of what the water supply system of Mostar was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked a question about water going to the east side. We talked briefly about the bridges and how they would have the water pipes, and I take it from your answers is that the water has to flow into the west side in order to go into the east side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, having reviewed these documents, first of all, do you know the gentleman that authored these letters, a Mario Salavarda?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's also an architect, and he was the head of the municipal department concerned with urbanism and infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And having reviewed these documents, can you please in a phrase or two tell us, what is Mr. Salavarda trying to convey to Dr. Prlic? What seems to be the problem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He conveyed the information indicating the gravity of the problem. He tried to explain to him that they were practically unable to supply even the right bank with water due to the poor piping - the pipes were failing - and due to the problems with the water source at Studenac. However, in order to comprehend the gravity of the system, one needs to be familiar with the whole system. Mostar has two sources of water. One of it is gravitational, and the other are wells where pumps are used to pump the water up and to push it under pressure into town. The source of the River Radivoje [phoen] normally dries out in the summertime so that the system is unable to supply a fraction of town with water, which is why the other source, where the pumps are used, has to be brought in. In a word, he was pointing to the problems that they were constantly dealing with, with the shortcomings of the system, if you want. Generally speaking, both systems can be used to supply water to the town up until the level of the fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, why weren't they able to simply make the repairs, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main town pipeline bringing the water from the source to town passes through the settlement of Rastani, and along its entire length the pipeline was exposed to the fire coming from the Muslim army. Even across on the other bank of the river the pipeline was being damaged, and this is what happened. If at one point there is no more water in a section of the pipeline, and if you switch the water on to flow and you can't control the pipelines, then the great pressure that builds up within the piping causes the pipes to break, to rupture, because you don't have any control over the valves that should ease the pressure building up within. If you are unable to control all these various factors, and if you let the water flow through the piping without any control, the result of it is that the pipes rupture.
